title: Errors that you actually catch
summary: Terminating versus non-terminating errors, -ErrorAction and $ErrorActionPreference, try/catch/finally with specific exception types, and reading an error record properly.

steps.title: Two kinds of error
body: PowerShell has **non-terminating** and **terminating** errors, and `try`/`catch` only sees the second kind.
- **Non-terminating**: a cmdlet reports a problem with *one* item and carries on with the rest. `Copy-Item` with a
missing source, `Get-Item` on one bad path out of ten, `Remove-Item` on a locked file. The error is printed and
added to `$Error`, `$?` becomes `$false`, and **the script goes on to the next line**.
- **Terminating**: the statement stops. `throw`, exceptions from .NET methods (`[IO.File]::ReadAllText(...)`),
parse errors, and any error raised with **`-ErrorAction Stop`**.
```powershell
try { Copy-Item ./missing.csv ./out/ } catch { 'never printed' }                    # not caught!
try { Copy-Item ./missing.csv ./out/ -ErrorAction Stop } catch { "caught: $_" }  # caught
For a whole script, set **`$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'`** at the top: every error becomes terminating, so the
first failure stops the script (or jumps to your `catch`). For a single call where you *expect* failures, use
`-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` (or `Ignore`) on that call only, never for the whole script.

steps.prompt: What does this print to the output (ignoring the red error message itself)?
steps.explain: `Get-Item` writes a non-terminating error and the `try` block simply continues, so `catch` never runs. Add `-ErrorAction Stop` to `Get-Item` (or set `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'`) and the output becomes `caught`, `after`.

steps.title: The alert that never fired
prompt: `~/scripts/copy-reports.ps1` has a `try`/`catch` that should exit `1` (so the scheduler alerts) when the copy fails.
Last night the source folder was missing. Reproduce it:
Fix the script so a failed copy prints a line with `FAILED` and exits with a **non-zero** code, without printing
`copied`. A good run must still copy the three CSV files and exit `0`.

checks.name: a missing source fails loudly
checks.cmd: out=$(pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/copy-reports.ps1 -Source ~/reports/missing 2>&1); rc=$?; echo "$out"; echo "exit $rc"; test $rc -ne 0 && echo "$out" | grep -q FAILED && ! echo "$out" | grep -q '^copied'
checks.fail: With a missing source the script must print `FAILED ...` and exit non-zero, and not claim it copied anything.

checks.name: a good run still works
checks.cmd: rm -f ~/share/reports/*; pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/copy-reports.ps1 >/dev/null 2>&1; rc=$?; test $rc = 0 && test "$(ls ~/share/reports | wc -l)" = 3
checks.fail: A normal run should copy the three CSV files into `~/share/reports` and exit 0.

hints: The output says `copied reports to ...` and `exit code: 0` even though `Copy-Item` printed an error. Which kind of error was it?
`catch` only runs for terminating errors. `Copy-Item` reports a missing path as non-terminating.
Add `-ErrorAction Stop` to the `Copy-Item` line (or `$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'` right after `param()`).
explain: `exit 1` in a script run with `pwsh -File` becomes the process exit code, which is what Task Scheduler, CI and
monitoring look at. An uncaught terminating error under `pwsh -File` also exits with `1`. A script that ends
normally exits with `0`, even if non-terminating errors scrolled past: that is exactly how this alert stayed silent.

steps.title: catch, finally, and reading the error record
body: ```powershell
try {
$cfg = Get-Content -Raw $path -ErrorAction Stop | ConvertFrom-Json
catch [System.Management.Automation.ItemNotFoundException] { throw "Config $path is missing" }
catch [System.ArgumentException]                           { throw "Config $path is not valid JSON: $($_.Exception.Message)" }
finally { Remove-Item $lockFile -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue }   # always runs: success, error, or Ctrl+C
Inside `catch`, **`$_` is an `ErrorRecord`**. When a message is not enough, look at the whole record:
```powershell
$Error[0] | Format-List * -Force           # every property, including the exception chain
$Error[0].Exception.GetType().FullName     # the type to put in a catch [ ... ]
$Error[0].Exception.InnerException         # the real cause, often wrapped one level down
$Error[0].ScriptStackTrace                 # which line of which script
$Error[0].InvocationInfo.PositionMessage   # the command and a ~~~~ marker under it
`$Error` keeps the most recent errors of the session, newest first. `-ErrorVariable failed` (no `$`) collects one
command's errors into `$failed` for later reporting. Use **`throw`** to stop with your own message, and
**`Write-Error`** to report a non-terminating problem with one input and carry on.

steps.prompt: Which property answers the question about `$e = $Error[0]`?
pairs: Which exception type do I catch?

steps.title: One bad record in the export
prompt: `pwsh -File ~/scripts/import-orders.ps1` fails on today's web shop export, `~/data/orders.json`. Run it, then
investigate the error record in your session: `$Error[0] | Format-List * -Force`.
1. Write the **full type name of the inner exception** (the parser's own exception, one level under the one
2. The message says exactly which record is broken. Fix that record in `~/data/orders.json` (the amount was
meant to be twelve and a half), so the script prints `orders: 6, total: 800`.

checks.name: inner.txt names the parser's exception
checks.fail: `$Error[0].Exception.InnerException.GetType().FullName` gives the inner exception's type. Write exactly that into `~/answers/inner.txt`.

checks.name: the import works
checks.fail: After fixing the record, the script should print `orders: 6, total: 800`.

checks.name: only the broken amount changed
checks.fail: Order 4 (Tailspin) should have `"Amount": 12.50`, and the other orders must be unchanged (the check shows amounts in cents).

hints: Run the script in your session so `$Error` is yours: `& ~/scripts/import-orders.ps1`, then `$Error[0] | Format-List * -Force`.
The `Exception` line shows two exceptions: `System.ArgumentException` and, after `--->`, the inner one. `Path '[3].Amount', line 5` is the 4th record (arrays count from 0).
explain: In production you would not hand-edit the export: you would reject it with a clear message and tell the team that
produces it, because a decimal comma in JSON means their serializer uses the wrong culture. The habit that matters
is the investigation: the outer exception says *what* failed, the inner one *why*, and the message often says *where*.

steps.prompt: A job must never leave its lock file behind, whatever happens. Put it in order.
lines: if (Test-Path $lock) { throw 'Another run is in progress' }
steps.explain: Check and create the lock before `try`: if another run holds it, this run must not delete it. Everything after the lock is created goes in `try`, and `finally` removes it even when the work throws or someone presses Ctrl+C.
